metadata.title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance.
metadata.abstract_summary: Expert performance is predicted by cumulative hours of *deliberate* practice - effortful, feedback-guided, specifically targeted at correcting weaknesses, not mere repetition or unstructured experience - far better than by innate talent alone.

sections.heading: Bottom Line
sections.text: Expert performance is predicted by cumulative hours of *deliberate* practice - effortful, feedback-guided, specifically targeted at correcting weaknesses, not mere repetition or unstructured experience - far better than by innate talent alone.

claims.text: Expert performance is predicted by cumulative hours of *deliberate* practice - effortful, feedback-guided, specifically targeted at correcting weaknesses, not mere repetition or unstructured experience - far better than by innate talent alone.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Retrospective diary studies and structured interviews with violinists at the Berlin University of the Arts across skill tiers, correlating estimated cumulative deliberate-practice hours with performance level, cross-checked against similar patterns reported in chess and other domains.

claims.text: Retrospective diary studies and structured interviews with violinists at the Berlin University of the Arts across skill tiers, correlating estimated cumulative deliberate-practice hours with performance level, cross-checked against similar patterns reported in chess and other domains.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- Landmark and hugely influential; the qualitative finding (deliberate practice matters more than raw hours or experience) has held up across many follow-up domains.
- The popularized "10,000 hour rule" overstates what the paper itself claims - it argues practice is necessary, not that any fixed number of hours is sufficient.
- Later meta-analyses (notably Hambrick et al.) found deliberate practice explains a smaller share of performance variance outside music and chess than this paper's framing suggests, and the retrospective self-reported practice hours are a real methodological weakness the authors themselves acknowledge.
